KOSHAL, J. G. Mukhi:By this judgment we shall dispose of Criminal . Appeals Nos. 606 and 607 of 1979 both of which are directed against a judgment of a Division Bench of the High Court of Gujarat dated the 19th January 1979 upholding the conviction recorded against and 442 the sentences imposed upon the three appellants under section 22A of the Minimum Wages Act (hereinafter called the Act) in each of two cases by a Judicial Magistrate at Morvi. Some of the facts leading to the prosecution of the appellants are not in dispute and may be shortly stated. Appellant No. 3 is the Morvi Vegetable Products Ltd., a limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of vegetable oil and vanaspati in Morvi, Gujarat, India, and the Company is a subsidiary of the Gujarat State Government and is the sole proprietor of the Company.
not liable for any contravention of the Act or the rules framed thereunder.(a)According to the prosecution the factory run by the Company is an oil mill, an industry which is certainly covered by the Act.(b) The Company does not carry on the business of sale of the oil manufactured by it except as an operation incidental to the manufacture of vanaspati, e.g., when there is a breakdown of the machinery used for converting oil into vanaspat or when oil become surplus on account of a shift in the Government policy in regard to the percentage of oil to be , consumed by the company.(c) Under section 5 of the act committees were appointed by the Government from time to time to hold inquiries and advise it in respect of fixation or revision of minimum rates of wages for employees in various industries.(d) No representative of the vanaspi industry was taken on any of these committees nor was any questionnaire issued to any of the manufacturers of vanasati, with the result that the Company was not bound by the recommendations of those committees or decisions taken in pursuance of the Government.(e) In respect of oil mills rates of minimum wages were fixed under the Act by the government for three types of employees, namely, skilled, semi skilled and unskilled.(f) There were no committees appointed to the Government to make recommendations regarding fixation and revision of the minimum wages for these employees.(g) There was no committee appointed to advise the Company on the subject of fixation of minimum wage for various kinds of employees working in an oil mills.(h) Apart from these, there was no Committee appointed for the purpose of making recommendations regarding fixing and revision.(i) There is no committee set up for the purposes of fixing or revision to minimum wages.(ii) There are no committees set up to arrange for the services of other types of workers which shows that a vanaspiti manufacturing mill is different from an oil Mill. akes were being sold by the Company not merely as an operation incidental to the business of manufacturing vanaspati but in the regular course of business is a finding of fact and cannot be called in question.(a) The Company was issued a questionnaire in its capacity as an oil mill by the committee appointed by the Government.(b) It is not disputed that the company is not covered by any of the items enumerated in Part I of the Schedule to the Act.(c) It cannot, therefore, urge that it had no opportunity to pre A sent its case before the committee which made recommendations in regard to fixation and revision of minimum wages.(d) It could not have made any argument advanced on behalf of the appellants in this connection.(e) There is no opportunity for the Company to pre-A to make a case to the committee.(f) It was not necessary for the Committee to make recommendations to the Committee which made its case to be made recommendations.(g)A survey of the various relevant provisions of the Act may be useful at this stage.(h) The Schedule is in two parts.(i)Section 2 contains definitions.(ii)Clause (e) of that section defines an 'employer ' as a person who employs one or more employees in any scheduled employment in respect of which minimum rates of wages have been fixed under the Act or any other process or branch of work forming part of such employment.(iii)According to clause (g) of the same section a 'scheduled employment ' means any employment specified in the Schedule and the act or any process or branches of work form part of any employment.
In he result, therefore, both the appeals fail and are dismissed S.R. Appeals dismissed.

, WANCHOO, J.S.A.This petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenges the legality of the notification dated July 30, 1958, (hereinafter called the impugned notification), issued by the Government of India fixing the ex factory price per maund of sugar produced in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar.The petition has been, opposed by the Central Government.It has been supported by two sets of interveners consisting of sugar factories in these areas who did not join the petition.The case of the petitioners is that the (X of 1955).Section 3(1) of the (C) of 1955, was passed by Parliament in 1955, for the control of the production, supply and distribution of, and trade and commerce in, certain commodities, which included sugar.Section 2(2) further provided inter alia for controlling the price at which any essential commodity might be bought or sold.It was, however, prohibited by the Constitution to impose any price or maximum price on any commodity that might be sold at any time.Section 4(2)(b) was also prohibited by Section 4(1)(a) for the importation of certain essential commodities.Section 5(b) prohibited importation and export of essential commodities at any price.Section 6(c) forbade importation or export of certain commodities.In exercise of these powers, the central Government promulgated the Sugar (Control) Order, 1955, on August 27, 1955.
By section 3 of the Act, the Central Government was given the power, if it was of opinion that it was necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices, to provide by order for regulating or prohibiting the production, supply and distribution thereof and trade and commerce therein.Clause 4 of the Order gave power to the Central Authorities, by notification in the Official Gazette, to fix the price or the maximum price at which any sugar might be &old or delivered, and different prices might be fixed for different areas factories or different types or grades of sugar.It is also alleged that fixing of the price was arbitrary and did not take into account the cost of production of a large number of units in the country and that did not provide for a fair and equitable distribution of sugar in the Country at a price in any way related to the price of the factories were compelled to sell their products. It is contended on their behalf that the entire object of fixing the Price of sugar was (a) to make it available at a reasonable price to the consumer, and (b) to ensure adequate and smooth flow and supply of sugar which is an essential commodity for the life of the people to all parts of the country according to their needs and requirements, checking the speculative tendency of the market and destroying the creation of an artificial shortage by unscrupulous persons.The Government did not admit that the price fixed was arbitrary or arbitrary.It was contended on the behalf of the Government took all relevant factors into account in fixing the price.This was done in the interest of the general public in order that sugar might not be sold at a fair price. It was done to the effect of the public interest in order to maintain the supply of the basic commodities of sugar, and to ensure the smooth flow of sugar from the ex factory stage to the present market. control prices elsewhere; nor was it necessary to control prices beyond the ex factory stage as the prices in the whole.There was in the circumstances no question of discrimination or any unreasonable restriction on carrying on trade in sugar.The Government did not admit that the price fixed was below the cost of production generally.The impugned notification is illegal and invalid.The Act and the Order have been passed in the interest of the general public and the public for the control of the production, supply and distribution of sugarcane and the distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price.The Order has been passed under Section 3 of the Act and Section 5 of the Order. The Order has not been attacked on the ground that it is illegal or invalid.
There is no force therefore in this petition and it is hereby dismissed with costs.Petition dismissed.

N: Criminal Appeal No. 2 of 1951.1.This Was an appeal under article 134 (1) (c) of the Constitution from the Judgment and Order of the High Court of Rajasthan (Nawal Kishore C.J., and Mehta J.) dated 16th October, 1950, in Criminal Appeal no. 63 of Samvat 2005, revising an order of acquittal of the Sessions Judge, Jai pur, and the State of Sawal Jaipur and Gangapur, that being the appropriate appellate tribunal in that area.2.This was an appeal against the conviction of the appellant Rameshwar, for the offence under sec. 2.376 of the Indian Penal Code.3.The material facts are stated in the judgment.4.K.N. Aggarwala, forthe accused.5.G.S. Mathur.6.Jai purDecember 20.1953.BOSE J. delivered judgment as fol lows.7.A.J. agreed.8.FAZL ALI J. agreed with the judge.9.AJIPURDecember 21.1952.The appellant Ramehwar was charged with com mitting rape on a young girl Mst.Gangapur-Purni, eight years of age.He was committed to Sessions and was convicted by the As sistant Sessions Judge; Sawai Jipur, and sentenced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 250.838.
The first point taken before us related to the admissi bility of the evidence of the girl herself.The proviso to section 5 of the , prescribes that "Provided that where the witness is a child under twelve years of age, and the Court or person having authority to examine such witness is of opinion that, though he understands the duty of speaking the truth, he does not understand the nature of an oath or affirmation, the forego ing provisions of this section and the provisions of section 6 shall not apply to such witness, but in any such case the absence of an Oath or affirmation shall not render inadmis sible any evidence given by such witness nor affect the obligation of the witness to state the truth."The question is whether the opinion referred to must be formally recorded or whether it can be inferred from the circumstances in which the deposition was taken. "It is true that the proviso quoted above must be read along with section 118 of the Evidence Act and section 13 of the Oaths Act.It states that "In my opinion, an omission to administer an oath, even to an adult, goes only to the credibility of the witnesses and not his competency. "The question of competency is dealt with in section 118. It states "Every 381 witness is competent unless the Court considers he is pre vented from understanding the questions put to him, or from giving rational answers by reason of tender years, extreme old age, disease whether of body or mind, or any other cause of the same kind."It will be observed that there is always competency in fact unless the court considers otherwise. It is true a subsidiary object is to bring home to the witness the solemnity of the occasion and to impress upon him the duty to speak the truth and not admissibility.
I would dismiss the appeal and direct the appellant to surrender to his bail in accordance with the terms of his bond, serve out his sentence and pay the fine.FAZL ALI J.A.I agree.Appeal dismissed.

The respondent, Ghisa Ram, is a Halwai dealing in milk and milk products, including Dahi, and holds a licence for running his shop in Defence Colony in New Delhi.On September 20, 1961, the Food Inspector of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi visited the shop of the respondent and took a sample of curd of cow 's milk for the purpose of testing whether there was any adulteration.The curd was churned and divided into three equal parts.Each part was put in a separate bottle and sealed by the food Inspector.The samples were then sent to the Public Analyst who carried out the analysis of the samples.One of the bottles containing the sample of the curd taken was handed over to the respondent.The other bottle was sealed and sealed.Out of the two remaining samples with the Food Investigator, one was sent to The Public Analyst.The Public Analyst conducted the analysis on October 3, 1961.The Food Inspector gave a certificate on October 23, 1961 in which he noted that the fat content in the Curd was 11.6% and the non fatty solids were 7.3%.The proportion of fat content was 1.2 % below the prescribed standard.The standard prescribed by the Rules framed under the (No. 37 of 1954) (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") for curd and non-fat solids was.According to the Act, if a curd is to be prepared for examination, it must be prepared with a minimum of 3.
Learned counsel for the appellant drew our attention to a decision reported in Suckling vs Parker(1).
In this appeal, the main contention on behalf of the appellant was that, though, under the Act, a certificate of the Director of the Central Food Laboratory has the effect of superseding the report of the Public Analyst, the absence of such a certificate for any reason whatsoever will not affect the value and efficacy of the certificate given by the Public analyst. The appellant's argument was that the certificate issued by the Director was superseded by the report given by his Public Analyst.The appellant's arguments were as follows: 'The proposition put forward by the appellant appears to be correct. 'Under, section 13(3) of the Act and sub section (5) of section 13 of the act, there is a right vested in the appellant to have his certificate issued as final and conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein. 'The proviso to sub section 1 of section 1(5) is that there can be no doubt that any document purporting to be a certificate signed by the Chairman of the Board of Directors or by any person who signs or signs a certificate is a certificate. 'There is no doubt, however, that there is no question, that the Certificate of the Chairman shall supersede the report that was signed by him on the :basis of which he issues a Certificate. 'These provisions are, therefore, only applicable when, in fact, there being no certificate issued, the certificate is issued by him and the certificate supersedes the report contained in it. 'It is when the accused exercises this right that he is able to obtain a certificate from the Director that he issues the certificate. "This aspect is, however the question of the validity of the case against the appellant. "If, for any purpose, the Certificate is issued, it does not cease to be evidence of any reason, no certificate is due to the fact that it is superseding by the facts contained in the report. sequently, under section 13(2) of the Act, the right accrued to the respondent to have the sample sent for analysis only thereafter. The right vested in the respondent was granted by the Director of the Central Food Laboratory on May 23, 1962.Section 13(1) specifically mentions that the accused vendor may make the application "after the institution of a prosecution under the Act."
Bhargava, J. (1906)In these circumstances, the acquittal of the respondent was justified, and the appeal is dismissed.V.P.S. Appeal dismissed (1) [1906]1 K.B.527.(2) AJ.R. 1965 M.p. 180.

BOSE J. R.S. MANIThis is a petition under article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of habeas corpus.The petition was presented by Mr. B.R.V. S. Mani, an advocate of the Nagpur High Court, on behalf of Shrimati Vidya Verma and was directed against her father Dr. Shiv Narayan Verma of Nagpur.The matter was brought up for hearing in the High Court on 6 12,1954, also under section 491.2.The issue arose of a petition against the wife of the President of India.The question therefore arose of our power of attorney from the lady and when the office pointed out that be could not present a petition without producing the necessary authority he amended the petition and described himself as the next friend of the lady.The case was referred to the Court on the appointed date.When the matter first came up for reading we directed a notice to issue to the father but later the same day it was brought to our notice that the opposite party was not either the Union of India or a State, nor was it some official acting under the orders of one or the other, but a private person.The notice was sent out and the matter was adjourned until the next hearing on 6 13,1955.The answer was:No.The person was not a private party.He was a public servant.Accordingly, before the notice was send out we recalled it and set the matter down for further hearing.At the adjourned hearing, Mr.
After hearing Mr. Mani for a time we decided to fix a date for the hearing of a prelimi nary question only, namely, whether a fundamental right is involved when the detention complained of is by a private person and not by a State or under the authority or orders of a State.As the question that arises here has been discussed at length in two earlier decisions of this Court we need not examine the matter, in any detail.The fundamental right that is said to be infringed is the one conferred by article 21: the right to personal liberty.In A. K. Gopalan vs The State of Madras(1) four of the six learned Judges who were in that case held that the word "law" in article 21 referred to State made law and not to law in the abstract.They rejected the contention that this was the same as the due process clause in the American Constitution.They held that Article 21 does not refer to the fundamental right to life and liberty.Patanjali Sastri., J. (as he then was) said at page 204 that as a rule constitutional safeguards are directed against the State and its organs and that protection against violation of rights by individuals must be sought in the ordinary law; and section R. Das, J. dealing with the question of preventive detention said at Page 324 that article 21 protects a person against preventive detention by the executive without the sanction of a law made by the legislature.The principle was applied to article 21(f) (f) and 31 (1) by a Bench of five Judges in P. D. Shamdasani vs Central Bank of India(2) who held that in the case of rights of property by private individual is not within the purview of these articles, therefore a person whose rights of Property are infringed by a person must seek his remedy under the ordinary and not under article 32. ttempt was an application under section 100 of the Criminal Procedure Code made by the person who, according to Mr. Mani, is the husband of the lady in whose interests he says he is acting.The application was filed in the Nagpur High Court at Nagpur.It was filed on 10 9 1954 and asked for a search warrant for the recovery of the Lady.The court granted the search warrant on 10 10 1954 and the lady was allowed to go to her uncle.The same gentleman then applied to the High Court in Nagpur on 18 10 1954 under section 491 of the criminal Procedure Code.He was denied.The learned Judges examined the lady, who is 25 years old, in person, on 20 10 1954.On the strength of her statement, which they recorded, they held that she was not under any restraint either in the house or outside and so dismissed the application on 10 11 1954.The next day the lady appeared in person.She appeared again the next day and clarified this by saying that she had no discomfort in living with her father but was not at ease with him 987.She said, that she did not want to live with her uncle, this time on two successive days.The girl appeared again on 20 12 1954.She did not say that she wanted to live in the company of her father.She also said, "I have no discomfort with living with my father but I have no comfort in living in my father's company.I am comfortable with my uncle 987 and would have more peace of mind with her Uncle.
It is accordingly dismissed.”The application was dismissed and a revision filed against the order of dismissal also failed.This was allowed on 24 1 1955 and no order was made about costs.Mr. Mani said: “In the circumstances set out above, we feel this is a case in which he should be made to pay the costs personally.We dismiss the petition and direct that Mr. Manni pay the Costs of the opposite party personally in addition to those of the learned Attorney General and that he bear his own, also personally.

GUPTA, J.D.A common question arises for consideration in these two appeals relating to the mode of calculating fifteen days ' wages of a monthly rated employee under section 4(2) of the (hereinafter referred to as the Act)."It is not necessary to state the facts in any great detail.The appellant company was the respondent's employer.The respondent was a public limited company.In both cases the respondent was employed by the appellant company and the appellant, a private limited company, was his employer."In Civil Appeal No. 1088 of 1976 (Shri Digvijay Woollen Mills Limited appellant vs 66 Shri Mahendra Prataprai Kakkad respondent) the respondent ceased to be an employee on attaining the age of superannuation after completing 19 years of service.He resigned his job on the basis that his monthly wages had been deducted from his wages for 26 working days."The respondent company calculated the amount of gratuity payable to him on the ground that fifteen days' wages was half of the monthly wages last drawn by him.He was entitled to an additional sum as gratuity on the grounds that he was not entitled to any gratuity.""The appellant demanded that his salary be deducted from the amount payable by the respondent.
The learned Judges however gave reasons in support of the order made.
Section 4(2) provides: "For every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months, the employer shall pay gratuity to an employee at the rate of fifteen days ' wages based on the rateof wages last drawn by the employee concerned: Provided that in the case of a piece rated employee, daily wages shall be computed on the average of the total wages received by him for a period of three months immediately preceding the termination of his employment, and, for this purpose, the wages paid for any overtime work shall not be taken into account: Provided further that in- case of an employee employed in a seasonal establishment, the employers shall pay the gratuity at the Rate of seven days ' wage for each season." "Wages" has been defined in section 2(s) of the Act as follows: ""wages" means all emoluments which are earned by an employee while on duty or on leave and which are paid or are payable to him in cash and includes dearness allowance but does not include any bonus, commission, house rent allowance, overtime wages and any other allowance. "We are not inclined to interfere with the decision of the High Court because it seems to us that the appeal before us is by special leave. "The appellant company paid him gratuity calculating his daily wages by dividing his monthly wages by 30 and computing fifteen days' wages on that basis. The appellant company claimed an additional sum as gratuity and the basis of the claim was the same as in the other appeal. The appeal before the Controlling Authority accepted the respondent 's contention and the appellate authority affirmed his decision following the view taken by the Gujarat High Court. "It is not necessary to consider whether another view is possible. "In this case also the appellant company summarily rejected the petition made by the respondent company challenging the judgment of the authorities under the Act. verse. "It is not necessary to consider whether another view is possible."The High Court summarily dismissed the petition of the appellant in both the appeals before us and upheld the decision of the authorities under the Act."We are not inclined to interfere with the case of the High Court because it seems to us that the view taken by the authorities is not in any way unreasonable or perverse.
The appeals are dismissed, in civil appeal 480 of 1977 with costs, In civil appeal 1088 of 1976 this Court while granting special leave on September 22, 1976 had directed the appellant to pay the costs of the appeal in any event accordingly respondent Mahendra Prataprai Buch will be entitled to his costs.P.B.R. Appeals dismissed.

J.I have read the judgment prepared by my brother, Mahajan J., and generally agree with his conclu sions and reasonings, but, having regard to the arguments made by the respondents and the importance of the points raised, I wish to add a short judgment of my own.There are really three questions to be decided in this appeals, and they are as follows ; (1) Whether in any event section 4 of the above Act is ultra vires the Legislature of the State of Bombay; (2) Whether the Act Section 4 of Section 5 of Section 6 of Section 3 of Section 4 and of Section 7 of Section 8 of Section 9 of Section 11 of Section 10 of Section 12 of Section 13 of Section 14 of Section 16 of Section 17 of Section 19 of Section 18 of Section 15 of Section 20 of the Act; (3) Whether and in what event the Bombay Supreme Court has jurisdicion to try the suit.The First and the Third QuestionsThe first and the third questions have been answered by the High court in favour of the appellant.The second question has been answered in favor of the respondents.The Third QuestionsIn this Court, the appellant attacked the judgment of the high Court in so far as it concerns the second question, whereas the first respondent attacked it in so well as it claims the first two questions. items in entry 1 of List II, "administration of justice, constitution and organization of all courts except the Federal Court. MUDHOLKAR, J.P.A. -The State of Andhra Pradesh has come up in appeal against the order passed in revision by the high Court of Chandigarh.The Supreme Court of India quashing the charges framed against nine persons by Mr. Syed Firasath Hussain, Special Judge, Vijayawada.The revision petition was preferred by only two of those persons.The accused No. 1 Parthasarathi, who was a lower division clerk in the Central Excise Circle Office at Narasaraopet was in charge of the TP 1 permit books (transport permit) intended for issue to Central Excises Officers for granting permits to persons applying bona fide for licences to transport tobacco.According to the prosecution two of the books containing 25 permit forms each were found missing from the aforesaid office.
The Subordinate Judge, Vijayawada was appointed as Special Judge under the provisions of section 6 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 (II of 1952) to try offenses under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. See. Section 5.5(2) of Act 11 of 1947 and See.Section 5(1)(d) of the Crime Prevention Act, 1948 and See, Section 5(3) of this Act, 1949, See. section 5(4) of that Act, 1946 and See., Section 5 (1)(a) of Section 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1947,See. Section 6.5.1 of the Act.CHARGE TO. 1.1.200 Mr. Umrigar, who appears for the State of Andhra Pradesh, while conceding that Charge No. 1 as it stands, is involved and obscure and requires to be reframed takes exception to the observation of the High Court that the charge is bad for multiplicity. He says,It not quite clear what the High court me ant.The High Court pointed out that this is an omnibus charge containing as many as 203 offenses and that it is 'in direct violation of sections 234, 235, 235 and 239 of the Penal Procedure. 'No doubt, sub section 2314(1) provides that separate charges should be framed for different offenses there can be no objection; but if it meant that all these accused cannot be tried at the same trial then we have no doubt that it was in error. The High Court also pointed out the fact that the accused persons cannot be charged with and tried at one trial for every such offence. No doubt, this is a multibus charge which is in direct contradiction to the provisions placed by Section 2314 (1) and Section 2315(1).
The view of the High Court is thus erroneous and its directions with respect to these offences are set aside.In the result we allow the appeal and set.aside the order of the high Court and direct the Special Judge to, frame fresh charges and proceed with the trial.The matter has been pending for a long time and we direct that the trial will proceed with.the trial.all expeditiously.Appeal allowed.Retrial ordered.

SAWANT, J.S.A.(1)Leave granted.(2)The only question which falls for consideration in the present case is what is the meaning of "Implementation Machinery" within the Meaning of the Code of Discipline (hereinafter referred to as the "Code") ratified by all Central Employers ' and Workers ' Organisations at the 16th session of the Indian Labour Conference held in May 1958 and which came into force from June 1, 1958.(3)What is the definition of Implementation Machinery under the Code?The question assumes importance in the Present case because the High Court by the impugned decision has held that since the appellant Union had addressed its application for recognition not to the implementation Machinery but to the Implementation Officer, the same was not properly made and the Implementation officer had no authority to initiate the process of recognition.(4)The admitted facts are that the appellant Rourkela Sramik Sangh had addressed a letter on October 9, 1989 to the Implement and Evaluation Officer cum Labour Comissionner Orissa, Cuttack intimating him that as per the Code it had called upon the Rourkeli Steel Plant to recognise it as the sole bargaining agent in the Plant, but that the Plant had not replied to the same.(5)The appellant in the said letter had further requested the Labour Commissioner to pass orders for immediate verification of the membership of all the trade unions operating in thesaid Plant and to recommend for recognition, the Union having majority of the members. charge of a Joint Secretary.In the State also, Implementation Units have been set up under the charge of either a whole time officer of the Labour Department or of the State Labour Commissioners.The Implementation Officer in each State is responsible for the implementation of the Code of Discipline.According to the recommendations of theLabour Ministers ' Conference held in January, 1960 the Implementation Officer of each State should, as far as possible, he whole time and of sufficient seniority.
The relevant provisions of the Code are as follows: Section IIof the Code deals with "Implementation Machinery" and is headed as such. The following functions have been assigned to 403 Implementation Units: (1) to ensure Implementation of the Codes of Discipline, Code of Conduct, labour enactments, awards, agreements, etc., with a view to reducing at the source the main cause of industrial strife; (2) to supplement the work of the Industrial Relations Machinery in taking preventive action where disputes are brewing and in settling long pending disputes which could not be settled otherwise; (3) to maintain liaison with Central, State or local units, as the case may be, to ensure effective working of the implementation machinery; (4) to arrange meetings of Implementation Committees and to function as their Secretariat; (5) to bring about out of court settlement of cases pending in High Courts and the Supreme Court; (6) to provide that cases are screened by the Screening Committees set up by the Central Employers ' and Workers ' Organisations before appeals are filed in higher courts; (7) to evaluate; (a) major strikes, lock outs and disputes in order to fix responsibility for them, and (b) the working of important Labour legislations, awards and policies, decisions, etc. (c)in order to see how far they have produced the results which they were intended to produce and suggest measures to improve them. The Code then deals with the following functions: 403 "(ii) Implementation Committees: 6.5"The Implementation Committees at the Centre and in the States represent both Central employers' and Workers' Organisations. The Implementation Committees are responsible for the following:The Central Implementation and Evaluation Committee consists of an equal number of employers ' and workers ' representatives four each from the Central employers 'Organisations. They are nominated by the organisations to which they belong and not by Government .
For the aforesaid reasons we are of the view that the High Court has erred in allowing Writ Petition No. 4426 of 1989 filed by the Ist respondent and dismissing the appllant 's Writ Petition being No. 361 of 1990.We, therefore, set aside the decision of the High court and direct the Deputy Labour Commissioner to complete the process of verification of membership and the Labour Commissioner and the Party to complete all the proceedings of recognition as expeditiously as possible and preferably within four months from the receipt of this decision.In the circumstances of the case, the parties will bear their own costs.R.S.S Appeal allowed.

BAHARUL ISLAM, J.P. 1, 1968.This appeal by special leave has been directed against the judgment and order passed by the Allahabad High Court dismissing two appeals filed by the appellants before it.The appellants were convicted under Sections 302, 307 and 323 all read with Section 149 of the Penal Code.They were sentenced to imprisonment for life, each, under Section 302/149, rigorous imprisonment for 7 years, each and under Section 307/149 and rigorous imprisonment of six months, each.The sentences were directed to run concurrently.Appellants Harish Chandra and Nathu were further convicted under Section 148 of the penal Code and sentenced to death for two years.The sentence of Nathu was also dismissed by the High Court as earlier stated.The facts material for the purpose of disposal of this appeal may be stated thus.The prosecution alleges that there was a long standing enmity between the parties of the deceased and the appellant, Pahelwan, in connection with the aforesaid incident.Some time prior to the incident a flour mill was installed and a house constructed by P.W. 1.Pahelwan had some vacant land in his possession.The appellant, Ram Swarup (deceased) objected to this.
Learned counsel for the appellants submitted that large number of injuries had also been received by the appellant and that there was no finding by the courts below as to how the assault was initially started and which party was the aggressor.
As such, he submitted, the conviction for the offences with the aid of Section 149, Penal Code, was bad in law.This Court in A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 2263 has held: (1) That the prosecution has suppressed the genesis and the origin of the occurrence and has thus not presented the true version; (2) that the witnesses who have denied the presence of the injuries on the person of the accused are lying on most material point and therefore their evidence is unreliable; (3) that in case there is a defence version which explains the injuries, and therefore it is rendered probable so as to throw doubt on the prosecution case.It is therefore, not correct to suggest as contended by the learned counsel for the defence version of the case, in view of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and the deceased that the injuries are serious.The defence version is not warranted by the findings of the High Court.The trial Court has found that the trial Court is not justified by the evidence presented by the witnesses.The omission on the part of the defence has been rendered probable by the fact that the evidence consists of interested or inimical witnesses or where the defence gives a version which competes in probability with that of the prosecutors one.The injury is serious.It has been established by the testimony of the witnesses that the injury is not serious. It has been proved that it is not a serious injury.The appellants had the right of private defence, and hence, they have committed no offence.The High Court agrees with the trial court.The submission of the Learned Counsel has not warranted the submission of a learned counsel.The Court agreeing with the Trial Court has held that the defence case is true.The case is not false.The evidence is not true.It was established by evidence of evidence of witnesses. The High Court agreed with the prosecution.
The submissions of learned counsel for the appellants do not stand scrutiny.This appeal has no merit and is dismissed.

CHANDRACHUD, CJ.(1) An important question arises for consideration in these two writ petitions.That question is whether a delay exceeding two years in the execution of a sentence of death must be considered sufficient for setting aside that sentence.(2) The petitioners are entitled to demand that the sentence be quashed and substituted by the sentence of life imprisonment.(3)Learned counsel who appears on behalf of the petitioners relies upon a decision of this Court in T.V. Vatheeswaran vs The State of Tamil Nadu(1b) and contends that since more than two years have passed since the petitionerers were sentenced to death by the Trial Court, they are not entitled to request that the said sentence should be revoked, substituted by a said sentence, or by the death sentence.
The question which arose for consideration in Vatheeswaran is formulated by Chinnappa Reddy, J., who spoke for the Court, in these terms: "But the question is whether in a case where after the sentence of death is given, the accused person is made to undergo inhuman and degrading punishment or where the execution of the sentence is endlessly delayed and the accused is make to suffer the most excruciating agony and anguish, is it not open to a court of appeal or a court exercising writ jurisdiction, in an appropriate proceeding to take note of the circumstance when it is brought to its notice and give relief where necessary ?" This question arose on the following facts as stated in the judgment of Brother Chinnapp Reddy: (1) The prisoner was rightly sentenced to death. (2) The sentence was imposed on account of the time factor alone, however right the death sentence was at the time when it was originally imposed. (3) "We do not doubt that this court has power, where there has been inordinate delay in executing death sentence in cases which come before it, to allow the appeal in so far as the death death sentence is concerned and substitute a sentence of transportation for life on accountof the time factors alone, which are not relevant to the circumstances of the case. (4) "But this is a jurisdiction which very closely entrenches on the powers and duties of the executive in regard to sentences imposed by courts. (5) "It is not an authority which any court should be slow to exercise. (6) "The executive should not exercise it in these cases. (7) "Except in Case No. XLVII (in which we are commuting the sentence largely for other reasons as hereafter appears), the facts of the crimes were such that if the death penalty which was the only sentence that could have been properly imposed originally, is to be commuted, we feel that it is for the executive to do so. cording to the rulings of this Court."
But, in that rare and exceptional class of cases wherein that sentence is upheld by this Court, the judgment or order of this Court ought not to be allowed to be defeated by applying any rule of thumb.This Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition filed by the petitioners on March 5, 1979.The last of the two Special Leave Petitions filed by them was dismissed by the same Court on August 24, 1981.The Court said, “A self imposed rule should be followed by the executive authorities rigorously, that every such petition shall be disposed of within a period of three months from the date on which it is received.”Delay defeats justice.“In the meanwhile, notice will go to the Government of Punjab.

Differing from both the courts below the High Court held that the cheque which the defendants had sent to the plaintiffs in payment of the amount in arrears within a month of the service of the writ of summons on him amounted to a valid tender of rent as required by section 13, and in view of section 12(3) no order for eviction could be made.The court held that there was no need for eviction of a tenant on the ground of default if the tenant made payment or deposits rent.The Court held: "The question is as to whether the payment of rent by cheque is valid tender or not. . . ."The question there was, whether a tenant whose tenancy had been terminated had any right to sublet the premises. The court held:"In the highly deveined and loped society, payment of cheque has become more convenient mode of discharging one 's obligation. The question there is, whether there is any power of subletting or not."The court stated: "If a cheque represents and produces cash, there is no reason why the payment should be accepted. There is no law of the common law, and the question there should be followed in deciding the question of whether the handing over of the cheques is not a sufficient tender of a rent if it is drawn for that amount. "The court said: "It is no doubt true that the issuance of the Cheque does not operate as a discharge of the obligation unless it is encased, and it is treated as a conditional payment, yet, in my view, this is not dishonoured. The Court said that the payment is a payment of cash. "In the present day society, I am of the view, an implied agreement should be inferred that if a payment is made by a checheque, that mode of payment would be admitted.

Khanna, J.S.An order was made by the District Magistrate Burdwan on February 10, 1971 under section 3 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970 (President 's ,Act No 19 of 1970) for the detention of Abdus Sukkur "with 681 a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order".The order was issued on February 11, 1971.The petitioner was arrested on September 24, 1971 and he was taken into custody on September 25, 1971 by the State Government under section 2 of the Act, 1971 (Act No.19 of 1970).Abdus Skkur thereupon filed the present petition through jail under article 32 of the Constitution to challenge his detention.The petition was heard on May 11, 1972.Mr. Chibber argued the case amicus curiae on behalf of the petitioner, while the State of West Bengal was represented by Mr. Chatterjee.The case was taken up thereafter on May 24, 1972 by the Supreme Court of India.After hearing the learned counsel on May 25, 1972 1 ordered that, for reasons to be given later, the petitioner be set at liberty.The Court said, "I now proceed to set out those reasons.The Petitioner was detained on September 23, 1971."The Order for the Detention of the Petitioner, as mentioned earlier, was approved by the Central Government.
As the above delay in considering and rejecting the representation had not been explained in the affidavit which was initially filed in.(1)It would thus follow that The delay on the part of the State Government in considering the representation of the petitioner has remained unexplained.(2)This unexplained delay, in my opinion, is sufficient to invalidate the detention of the petition.(3)According to clause (5) of article 22 of the Constitution, when any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be practicable, notify to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order.(4)The fact that earliest opportunity has to be afforded to the detent for making a representations against the detention order necessarily implies that, as and when the representation is made, it should be dealt with promptly.(5)The requirement about the giving of earliest opportunity to a detenu to make a representation is a farce and empty formality.(6)It is, therefore, essential that there should be no undue or unexplained delay in disposing of the said representation.(7)This is as it should not be, because it would run counter to the underlying object and the requirement for the consideration of the representation made by the said person.(8)It should be noted that "the requirement about not giving any earliest opportunity for a detent to be made and to give any earliest chance to a person to make an representation against a detention order would plainly be reduced to a Farce and Empty formality if the authority concerned after giving such an opportunity pays no prompt attention to the representation which is submitted by the detenue as a result of that opportunity.(9)The authority concerned has a duty to act strictly in accordance with law. nt authorities. It was held that "No definite time can be laid down within which a representation of a detenu should be dealt with save and except that it is a constitutional right of adetenu to have, his representation considered as expeditiously as possible. It is the duty of the Government to consider and dispose of his representation as soon as possible." It was also held that the Government was guilty of the infraction of the constitutional provision because of inordinate delay in considering the representation. "Reliance in the case of Jayanarayan Sukul vs State of West Bengal (supra) was placed upon an earlier decision of this Court in the, case of Khairul Haque vs Stateof West Bengal, (W. P. No. 246 of 1969 decided on September 10, 1969). Reliance in that case this Court held that article 22(5) of the Constitution envisaged a dual obligation of the State Government and a corresponding dual right in favour of a Detenu, namely, (1) to have his representation independently considered by the Government, and (2) to make that representation, in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, considered by an Advisory Board.
The petitioner was accordingly set at liberty.I therefore, accept the petition and make the rule absolute.V.P.S. Petition allowed.

RANGANATH MISRA, J.S.A.The following is a list of appeals filed in the Karnataka High Court.These are appeals by special leave, the first one by Nagaraja, the main contestant, and the second by the State of Karnataka challenging the decision of the Karn Karnataka State Administrative Tribunal by which the Tribunal accepted the claim of inter se seniority of re spondent No. 1.Nagaraja was appointed as Deputy Director in the Youth Services of the State on 27th of March, 1978.In the Directorate of Youth Services, there are posts of Assistant and Deputy Directors.There are two posts of Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors in the Directorate.Appellant Nagaraj joined service under the State Government as a Lecturer on 6.9.1966 and came on deputation as Editor of 'Youth Karnataka ' from 18th of August, 1976.While working as such Editor he was confirmed in the office of the Deputy Director on 13th of April, 1978, while working as an Editor of the Youth Directorate.On 13.8.1978, he was promoted to Assistant Director and was confirmed as a Deputy Director for a period of six months.On 14th of October, 1978 and on 20th of November, 1978 he was transferred to Deputy Director.On 16th of December, 1978 it was announced that he was to be promoted to the position of Deputy Director and on 22.12.1978 his appointment was made on regular basis with effect from 27.3.1978.
The order of December, 1978, could not provide a regular retrospective promotion in view of the special Rules obtaining in the State.Thereupon, these two ap peals have been filed one by Nagaraja and the other by State of Karnataka.Nagaraja was appointed Deputy Director of Youth Services on 13th of October, 1978.His regular promotion was notified on 20th of September, 1978 and he was promoted to Deputy Director on 21st of October.Therefore, the Tribunal has not accepted Nagaraj as Deputy Director between 13th OF October and 20th Of October.The Tribunal has also not accepted Gudodagi as a direct recruit from 7.8.1978.To meet that situation the notification of 22nd December,1978.had been made, which read thus: "In continuation of Government Notification . . dated 6th of March, 1978 dated 27.3.1978, Sri N. Nagnaraja, Assistant Director of youth Services is regularly promoted to officiate as Deputy Direc tor of Youth Service with effect from 27th April, 1978 to 27th May, 1978 (i.e. date from which he was confirmed as Assistant Director) . " The Tribunal has found that under Karnataka State Civil Services (Regulation of Promotion, Pay & Pension) Act, 1973, no retrospective promotion is admissible unless the situa tion comes within the various clauses of rule 2.1.The in stant case, according to the Tribunal, was not covered by rule 2 and, therefore, the order of22nd of December., 1978, giving a retrospective promotion from 27. 3.1978 was not justified.The tribunal has also concluded that there is no need for a retrospective notification.Once that notification goes, Gudadagi being a direct hire from 7 and 8.9.1978 would be entitled to seniority.We have analytically examined the judgment of the Tribu nal with reference to the submissions made at the Bar.
The appeals are dismissed.There would be no order as to costs.N.V.K. Appeals disallowed.

FAZAL ALI, J.P.A.This is a defendant 's appeal by special leave against the judgment and decree of the High Court of Bombay dismissing its second appeal in limine by its order dated August 24, 1967.The appeal raises important and interesting questions of law relating to the interpretation of some of the provisions of the Indian Railways Act pertaining to the liability of the Railways for breach of contract.The plaintiff/respondent brought a suit for recovery of an amount of Rs. 2,378.65 nP being the damages for contract resulting from delayed delivery of the goods consigned by the plaintiff through the defendant Railways to be delivered at Poona.The case was filed before the District Judge of Bombay in toto and found that there was no inordinate delay in the delivery of goods to the plaintiff.
Secondly it was submitted that even if the case of the plaintiff does not fall within the four corners of section 76 of the new Railways Act, the common law right of the plaintiffs to claim damages against the appellant has not been barred by the Act.Thirdly it was also submitted that the plaintiff has not claimed interest on any specified amount of money but has merely calculated the same as a measure of damages which it suffered due to the breach of contract and gross negligence on the part of the Railways which has been found by the Courts below.There is also a public demand for such a change.
The Solicitor General, therefore, rightly contended that in cases falling squarely within the four corners of section 76 of the new Act, section 78(d) will apply.
Mr. Phadke appearing for the respondent has repelled the contentions of the appellant on the ground that the new Railways Act does not reduce or diminish the liability of the railway administration for breach of contract but in fact the Act seeks to increase the liability.The Law of the Indian Contract Act, 1890, Section 72(1) of the old Act ran thus: "The responsibility of the Railway administration for the loss, destruction or deterioration of animals and goods delivered to the administration to be carried by railway shall, subject to the other provisions of this Act, be that of a bailee under sections 151, 152 and 161 of the British Contract Act."In other words, the railway Administration was impressed with the duty to carry the goods with the same care and caution which a prudent owner would apply in the case of his own goods If there was any violation or breach of the said care and cautions expected of a Railway it would have been liable to damages."Section 72(2) was amended by section 72 of the new Act in order to make the responsibility of railway administration as a carrier of animals or goods subject to all the provisions of the English Contract Act and to make it a duty of a Bailee under section 151.(3) It may be pertinent to note that sub section (3) of section 72 was the same as section 151 of the existing Act, and that under section 71 of the same Act it was the duty of the railways to carry animals and other goods.(4) Section 72 (1) and (5) were the same provisions as the English contract Act.(6) The responsibility of a railway administration is clearly that of the bailee.(7) The responsibilities of the Railways in India shall be: "(1) A bailee shall carry animals or other goods delivered by railway.(8) A common carrier shall carry the same bulk, quality and value. s bailees, the railways are required to take as much care of the goods entrusted to them for carriage as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value."However, closely following the legal position in the United Kingdom, it is proposed that the basic responsibility of our railways for loss, destruction or deterioration etc.of animals or goods be as set out in the proposed section 73.(1) "When the railways assume this responsibility, broadly speaking, they will be liable for loss of or injury to goods while in transit by rail, arising from any cause whatsoever, unless such loss or injury is proved by the railways to have been caused by an act of God, or by an acts of war, or for any act of public enemies or is proved to be consequence of inherent vice in the thing carried or is attributable to the consignor 's own fault."(2) "Even where the loss is found by the roads to be caused by accidents or accidents, just referred to by me, and where the railways will not be absolved of their responsibility unless they further prove that they had used reasonable forethought and care in the carriage of animals and goods.(3) "It is well settled that the responsibility of the railways is to take the responsibility for the loss and injury to the goods carried by the railway."This is the clear background against which the new Act was passed.(4)"Even the statement of objects and reasons, the relevant parts of which may be extracted as under, shows the main object of the New Act: "The Railway Freight Structure Enquiry Committee (1956 57) has recommended that the Responsibility of the railway in India as carriers of animals or Goods, which is at present that of a bailee, should be changed to that of the common carrier. , however, unable to accept this argument.
We are, therefore, of the opinion that in view of the finding of fact arrived by the Courts below the plaintiff is undoubtedly entitled to damages This brings us to the second contention raised by the Solicitor General, namely, that the plaintiff cannot be entitled to interest as damages for breach of the contract. The Court has found that this is not the case and therefore dismissed the matter with costs.The fact of the matter is that it is not a matter of interest.The contention raising by the learned Solicitors General on this point is, however, overruled.The Court has concluded: “In these circumstances, Therefore, all the contentions raised by THE SolicIT General fail and we find no merit in this appeal which is accordingly dismissed with costs”.P.

[Diploma Holders and Graduates]These four Civil Appeals by Special Leave and the Special Leave Petition arise out of and are directed against the common Judgment dated 2.9.1987, of the High Court of Delhi in C.W.P. No. 2132 and C.M.P, No. 2082 of 1984 in which the principal controversy was whether the Rules prescribing different conditions of eligibility for Diploma HoldERS and Graduate for promotion from the cadre of Junior Engineers to that of Assistant Engineers and from the Cadre of Assistant engineers to that the Executive Engineers in the Public Works Department of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and would, therefore, require to be declared void.The High Court, in the writ petitions filed by the Diploma holders, has held that such differential treatment of Diabetic Holders, Graduates by the prescription of different standards of service experience for purposes of eligibility of promotion to the higher cadres is unconstitutional.The D.D., which is the appellant in Civil Appeals No.898 of 1988 and No. 899 of 1988 assails the correctness of the view taken by the Supreme Court.
Learned counsel for the appellants, contended that the view that commended itself to the High Court is demonstrably erroneous and is opposed to principles which, by now, should be considered well settled.But in the present case, counsel contended, that is not the position.
Learned counsel for the respondent diploma holders, while seeking to support the judgment of the High Court urged that this Court had, more than once, cautioned against undue accent, in the matter of promotional opportunities, on academic qualification alone which might lead to elitist preferences and tend to obscure the egalitarian principle and social justice.
CWP No. 2082 of 1984 pertained to the contitutionality of the analogous provisions in the rules adopted by resolution No. 105 dated 16.6.1971. The High Court held: "The principal question that arises in these appeals is whether, where, as here, recruitment to a particular cadre of posts is made, from two different sources, different conditions, based on the differences in educational qualifications, can be prescribed conditioning the eligibility for further promotion to a higher cadre in service. "The High Court, by the judgment now under appeal, has held that such prescription of differential standards on the basis of technical, educational qualifications is violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. "In reaching such conclusions as it did on the point, the High Court placed reliance on the pronouncement of this Court in Mohammad Shujat Ali vs UOI and Others,[1975] 1 SCR 449, H. C. Sharma and Ors. 2vs Municipal Corporation of Delhi, and Anr. 1vs Ravinder Kumar Sharma & Ors., ; and Punjab State Electricity Board,Patiala, and A. R. Sharma & Anr., and A R. R., v. Patiala and Others, v. Bihar, and v. Jammu & Kashmir, and V.R., v, Bihar, V.S., V. S., and R. J. Singh,[1986] 4 SCC 617 and T.R: Kapur and Others vs State of Haryana and Others. v. V. Singh, v., and v, V, V., V., and V., v., V, etc., etc. v, etc. etc.
Accordingly, all the Appeals are allowed, the Judgment of the High Court dated 2.9.1987 set aside and the Civil Writ Petitions No. 2 132 of 1984 and 2082 of 1984 in the High court dismissed.However, the parties are left to bear and pay their costs, both here and below.A.P.J . . .Appeals allowed.

Gopal deceased died on June 11, 1953, at about 10 p.m.This is an appeal by special leave against the judgment of the Allahabad High Court in a criminal matter.The facts of the case, as found by the High Court, are no longer in dispute and the 648 question that is raised in this appeal is whether the appellant had exceeded the right of private defence of person.The appellant was convicted under section 304, Part 11, of the Penal code and sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment.The relevant facts for our purposes are these.1.Gopal deceased was married to the sister of the appellant.2.The sister of Gopal was a member of a family in law.3.He was the appellant's brother Vishwanath.4.He and his father Badri were living in a railway quarter at Gorakhpur.5.He had been living with his father in law, who was also living in another railway quarter nearby.6.They did not, however, pull on well together and Gopal shifted to the house of Banarsi.7.Badri persuaded Gopal to come back to his house but the relations remained strained and eventually Gopal shifting again to the quarter of Banarasi about 15 days before the present occurrence which took place.8.The present occurrence took place on the night of June 11.The night of the night, Gopal 's wife had continued to live with her father as she was unwilling to go with Gopal.9. r of opinion that more harm than the circumstances of the case required was not caused; and therefore the appellant was also acquitted.The State then appealed to the High Court against the acquittal of both accused.
The Sessions Judge was further of opinion that the appellant had the right of private defence of person, and that this right extended even to the causing of death as it arose on account of an assault on his sister which was with intent to abduct her.The acquittal of the appellant was set aside on the ground that the case was not covered by the fifth clause of section 100 and the right OF private defence in person in this case did not extend to the voluntary cause of death to the assailant and therefore it was exceeded.The High Court relied on an earlier decision of its own in Emperor vs Ram Saiya (1). The appellant was acquitted on the grounds that he did not have the right to self-defence.He applied for a certificate to enable him to appeal to this Court but this was refused.The main question therefore that falls for consideration in this appeal is whether the decision in Ram (1) I.L.R. 1948 All.Shutterstock(2) The High Court has taken a view which is different on that taken in Emperor (1), namely Jagat singh vs King Emperor (2) Daroga Lokar vs Emperor Lohar vs The State (4) and Dayaram Laxman vs State 'here is, however, no discussion of the point in these our cases and we need not refer to them further.
We, therefore, allow the appeal and hold that the appellant had the right of private defence of person under the fifth clause of section 100 and did not cause more harm than was necessary and acquit him.Appeal allowed.

: Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 1620 of 1980.From the Judgment and order dated 13 11 1979 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No 1310 of 1979.Pramod Swarup for the Petitioner.M. C. Bhandare and M. N. Shroff for the Respondent.
The order of the Court was delivered by KRISHNA IYER J. We were not happy at the disposal by the High Court of a case under section 302 I.P.C. without a speaking order. We felt that the Court should have heard the case in a more reasoned manner.After all in so serious a crime as murder, where so severe a sentence as life imprisonment has been inflicted by the trial court and the appeal is as of right, the High court must indicate in a reasoned judgment that it has applied its mind to the material questions of fact and law.A judgment may be brief but not a blank, especially in a situation such as this.For this reason we should have straightaway set aside the judgment of the high Court and sent it back for fresh hearing, but under Article 136 where justice is the paramount consideration we wanted to reduce the delay in the proceedings since there is a sentence of life imprisonment on the petitioner so we directed that the original record be sent for so that counsel on both sides may 1195 have the opportunity to peruse the entire case records and make submissions to us as if we were hearing the appeal in the regular course.We also directed that counsel for the petitioner be allowed to make submissions after perusal of the materials. We also directed the court to send a copy of the case record to the Special Leave Petition Committee.After a brief hearing counsel for both sides was unable to demonstrate that the trial trial court 's judgment was vitiated by any flaw in appreciation of evidence or assessment of probabilities. We therefore decided to dismiss the case.We, therefore, dismiss the Special leave Petition after satisfying ourselves that natural justice has had its full play.
Dismissed. P.P.B.R. Petition dismissed.

Ahmed was a member of the Indian Administrative Service Cadre.He was posted as Deputy Commissioner and District Magistrate, Nowgong District.In that very year he was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner.He held the post until he retired from service in June 1960.The Government of Assam appointed him as the Deputy Commissioner in the District Magistrates' Court.He served till June 1960, when he resigned from the post.He retired from the office in the beginning of June 1960 at the end of the month of June.While he was holding the aforementioned post, some time in the early morning hours of the morning of June 30, 1960 there were large scale disturbances which occurred in Nowgongs city and District area described in official parlance as 'language disturbances '.There was considerable damage to property.There were also disturbances in other parts of the city and district as well as in the district.One Shri A. Kidwai, the then Additional Chief Secretary to the Government of Attam, undertook an inquiry into the causes of disturbances at NowgONG with a view to ascertaining the responsibility of District officials.He submitted his Report. mposed the penalty of removal from service on the respondent. ________________A memorial submitted by the respondent to the President under Rule 20 of the All India Services (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1955, ( 'Discipline and Appeal Rules ' for short), against the imposition of the penalty was rejected.________________________________________________The respondent filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Assam and Nagaland. ________________________________________________Two contentions were raised before the high Court: (1) Whether rule 16(2) of the Retirement Rules is attracted so as to retain the respondent in service beyond the period of his normal retirement for the purpose of completing disciplinary proceedings against the respondent; and (2) if rule 16[2) was not attracted, whether the retention of respondent beyond the normal period of the retirement was valid and if it was not valid, whether he 508 could be removed from service after he had actually and effectively retired from service ?
To appreciate the contention it is better to have a look at the charges framed against the respondent.The expression 'devotion to duty ' appears to have been used as something opposed to indifference to duty or easy going or light hearted approach to duty.
One such penalty prescribed therein is 'removal from service which shall not disqualify for future employment '. Rule 4 prescribes the authority competent to institute disciplinary proceedings. Where a member of a service has committed any act or omission which renders him liable to any penalty specified in rule 3, an inquiry shall be held according to procedure prescribed in rule 5.    The disciplinary proceedings shall be conducted according to the procedure prescribed by rule 3.    Discipline and Appeal Rules provide for disciplinary action and imposition of penalties. A survey of these rules would show that disciplinary proceedings can be held against a member member of the service for any acts or omission committed by him which, according to rule 2, must provide good and sufficient reason to impose one or the other of the penalties mentioned therein. Execution of any act, omission or commission is prohibited by rule 4 of the Discipline and Appeal ( 'Discipline & Appeal Rules ' for short) and is punishable by a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment. Sub rule (2) of rule 16 of Rule 16 of the Retirement Rules enables the Government to put under suspension a member or the Service during disciplinary proceeding if having regard to the nature of charges and circumstances the Government thinks it proper to do so. An examination of the rules and the conduct of the disciplinary proceeding is required to provide for the imposition of a penalty and such penalty can be imposed. In the case of a delinquent officer under suspension, the disciplinary proceedings may be thwarted and the Government may have to take personal control of the proceedings and the consequences of such disciplinary proceeding are likely to be thwarted.
The High Court was, therefore, right in coming to the conclusion that the respondent was no longer in service on the date on which an order removing him from service was made and, Therefore, the order was illegal and void.Accordingly, this appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.P.B.R. Appeal dismissed.

Garg.The adventurous petitioner imaginatively challenges the vires of Section 7 read with Section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and the relevant rules framed thereunder.The gravamen of his charge is that the above provisions, read together, impose an inflexible minimum sentence of six months R.I. of offender 's guilty of sale of adulterated food, excluding in the process even the need to prove mens rea in the accused.This absolute liability, with mandatory sentence, dependent on sophisticated chemical tests and complicated formulae, is oppressively unreasonable in the illiterate, agrestic realities of little Indian retail trade.The primary props to support this broad submission may be briefly noticed.There is no such thing as a fair trial.Nor is there any intelligent differentiation between petty dealers and giant offenders, and vendors, big and small, are put on the Procrustean bed of stern punishment alike.This is not the case.This case is not a case of petty theft.
Counsel complains that there is no classification as between injurious pollutants and innocuous adulterants while proscribing the sentence as between the two categories of pollutants and the sentence is not the same.
Such, in one sentence, is the submission of counsel.(Articles 14, 19 and 21 are the constitutional artillery employed by counsel to shoot down the said provisions of the Act. )Frankly, we are not impressed with the consternation about the constitutionality even if the potential for victimisation affecting smaller people may be real and elicit our commiseration.(We may dwell for a moment on the latter grievance against the law a little later. )First, we will repel the vice of unconstitutionality.(Let us be clear about the basics.(Policy is for Parliament, constitutionality for the Court. )Protection of public health and regulation of noxious trade belong to the police power of the State and legislation like the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is of that genre.(If a sentence, as here, is prescribed as a mandatory minimum and that is too cruel to comport with article 21 and too torturesome to be reasonably justifiable or socially defensible under article 19 then a case for judicial review may arise.(It is a matter of judicial discretion in constitutionality. )But we see none here.-Nor can we agree that judge proof sentencing is per se bad.-Sometimes judicial discretion is used to ensure that fluctuations in punishment, especially on the softer side where white collar criminals are involved, induce legislative standardisation of sentences, to avoid giving societal protection in hostage to fortune.-There is a wide play still left for the court, and mandatory minima are familiar from the days of the Penal Code (Vide Sec. 302).-The prescription of equal protection is not breached either, because within the range of legislative discretion the court deals out to each what he deserves according to established principles.-Shri R. K.
We dismiss the Writ petition since there is no constitutional invalidity made out and the grounds urged are more appropriately an appeal to the Parliament and the Executive.V.D.K. Petition dismissed.

Chidambaram, K.Parasaran, M.N. Krishnan, G. Srinivasan, B.Rabu Manohar G.Vijay Anand, V. Balachandran and Ajit K. Sinha for the Respondents.The Order of Appeal No. 1761 61 of 1991 was delivered and the following order was delivered by the Court: Leave granted.
Since the Division Bench,issued the impugned orders following the judgment of the Full Bench, the impundned orders are not sustainable in law and are not applicable to the court of law.
The Division Bench following the decision of the Full Bench in Writ Petition No. 2712 of 1990 and other connected matters (fathima Secondary Grade Teachers Training Institute vs Commissioner and Secretary to Government, Education Department), issued similar directions permitting the student to appear at the examination and directing the State Government to arrange for supplementary examination to enable the students to appear on that examination.The Full Bench observed that there is no dispute that the respondent educational Institutions were established for imparting education in Teachers Training Course without obtaining recognition from the Education Department of the State government.The Court observed that the students pursuing their studies in these Institutions could not be granted relief in the public examination held by the Government.the Full Bench noted these decisions and observations and yet is granted relief to the students of unrecognized educational institutions.The High Court was persuaded to issue directions on humanitarian ground which were in effect destructive of its own findings, and the law laid down by it.The court observed that these directions in our opinion were unauthorised and wholly unjustified. The Full Bench rightly held that there was no dispute in the petitioners’ case that the appellant authorities were not entitled to make a special provision for supplementary examinations.The full Bench was persuaded by the High Court to grant relief to these petitioners on humanitarian grounds.The view of the Court was that the Court should have refused relief to all the parties involved in the matter. The view of this Court was vindicated by the Court’s own findings and observations.The views of the full Bench were vindicated.The opinion of the court was vindictive.The principle of the rule of law was violated. The principle of freedom of expression was violated by this Court.
We, accordingly, allow the appeals and set aside the order of the High Court and dismiss the writ petitions filed by the respondents.There will be no order as to costs.G.N. Appeals allowed.

VENKATARAMIAH, J.P.A.—This appeal by special leave is filed against the judgment of the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Appeal No. 174 1972 convicting the appellant, Dara Singh, of an offence punishable under section 23F of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 (Act No. 7 of 1947) (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') and sentencing him to imprisonment for a term of one year with a direction that the said sentence should be served by him concurrently with the sentence of imprisonment for life imposed on him in another case on a charge of murder. The appellant has pleaded not guilty to the said offence. The facts leading to this appeal can be summarised thus: On March 28, 1963 foreign currencies amounting to $ 185 and U.S. $ 13060 besides Indian currency equivalenting to Rs. 1,300 were seized from the appellant by the Railway Police at the Railway Station at Sangrur.
For proving the guilt of Dara Singh in the light of the charge framed against him, it had only to be established that he had failed to pay the penalty imposed by the Director of Enforcement.
The relevant part of the judgment of the High Court reads thus: "The order of acquittal made by the learned trial Magistrate proceeds, in our opinion, on an altogether erroneous view of the provisions of section 23F of the Act. Accordingly, the Director of Enforcement should have paid the penalty within 45 days from 991 the said date. "Obviously, however, no payment could be made unless the person on whom the penalty was imposed had come to know about the order. "He should have, therefore, paid the sentence within a reasonable period from that date and in any case within 60 days from the same date."The penalty not having been paid or deposited by Dara Singh, he was clearly guilty of contravention of the adjudication order made by a Judge of the Court and should have been, convicted under section 23(1) of the same Act. "The question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the Court was right in the circumstances of the case in finding the appellant guilty of the offence in question. "It is necessary at this stage to refer briefly to some of the terms of the application and the Adjudication Proceedings and Appeal Rules, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Rules ') framed under section 27 of the act.
In the result, the appeal is allowed and the conviction of the appellant and the sentence imposed on him by the High Court are set aside.The order of acquittal passed by the Magistrate is restored.It is not known whether the appellant was in fact released on bail pursuant to the above order.If he is on bail, his bail bond stands cancelled.P.B.R. Appeal allowed.
